messages.subject: finishing a covariance function implementation (for GPs)
parts:
Hi folks. Daniel and I have been hoping to find time to finish up his
implementation of the squared exponential (aka RBF aka exponentiated
quadratic) kernel. Anyone have some time to help us? Basically we just
need to finish the tests--and the reason we haven't done that is I
haven't (yet) got my C++ skills up to speed while Daniel's been busy
with other stuff. Here's the branch:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/tree/feature/issue-191-gp-squared_exponential

The tests we need are:

test/unit/math/prim/mat/fun/cov_sq_exp_test.cpp
test/unit/math/prim/scal/fun/squared_distance_test.cpp
test/unit/math/fwd/mat/fun/cov_sq_exp_test.cpp
test/unit/math/fwd/scal/fun/squared_distance_test.cpp
test/unit/math/rev/mat/fun/cov_sq_exp_test.cpp
test/unit/math/rev/scal/fun/squared_distance_test.cpp

(Help could certainly consist of someone spending time on a hangout
with me getting me up to speed with the C++ I don't know...)

And attached are some worked out numeric evaluations that we can use
to implement the tests.

Daniel, please correct anything I've gotten wrong.

Seth

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] finishing a covariance function implementation (for GPs)
parts:
Hi all,

I'm back! The code is complete without any optimization of the gradients. Before it's ready, it needs the tests Seth mentioned.

Seth and everyone else, writing tests isn't about C++ code. It's all about being willing to be careful and do a little bit of work. If all you did was in a document put down inputs and outputs, then coding those are trivial. It's generating enough test cases and the combinations under which we would instantiate the code that matters.

The reason I want this to be well tested first is we will want to make this faster. Once we get into the territory of writing custom derivative code for operators, it is immensely helpful to have existing tests that we know work. It's really hard to get code right the first time.

Seth forwarded the analytic gradients (sorry -- I meant to forward that to the list, but I sat on it). What we should do is in any format you want (but a test is best), write out:
- input. Something like: (x data = [1, 2, 3], sigma data = 1, lambda data = 1), (x var = [1, 2, 3], sigma var = 1, lambda var = 1)
- output. Something like: cov_mat = [3x3 matrix], dcov_mat[1,1] / d_x[1] = ?, dcov_mat[1,2] / d_x[2] = ?, ..., dcov_mat[1,1] / d_sigma, ...

And we have to hit the edge cases. So... sigma = 0. lambda = 0. sigma = inf...


I have a few more high priority things going on. I've tested it a little bit, but we need more tests. If you want to help, just write down sets of input and output and we can code that into tests easily. Would it help if I put in a skeleton test to show you how it's done? I don't know how much more I can do to get those that are interested in just writing down test cases.


Daniel

On Monday, May 23, 2016 at 5:13:19 AM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Devin doesn't know C++ yet and this one's hairy or Daniel would be

> bogging down the vectorization.

And my guess is that with enough functions vectorized, the covariance matrix computation could be fully vectorized when written in Stan language so that the expression tree would be smallish and it would be quite fast even without internal C++ implementation of the covariance function...

Aki

Ah, I see them now.

That's a start, but there's a lot more to do. We also need the cases where there is only one input variable x.

Having it in a condensed form would be useful. For the tests, unless we're implementing the analytic gradient as a function, we only need the values. Maybe we should implement that analytic gradient in the test? That would be the most useful.

But there's a lot more like what happens when x1 is length 2 and x2 is length 3? Or the other way around? (I know what "should" happen, but does the code actually do that?... I hope so, but these are things that a quick typo in the code could mess things up.) What happens when x1 is length 0? And perhaps a case where x1 and x2 are fairly large would be useful.


Daniel

parts:
> On May 23, 2016, at 4:04 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:

> On Monday, May 23, 2016 at 5:13:19 AM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Devin doesn't know C++ yet and this one's hairy or Daniel would be
>> done with already. All these higher-order tests are also what's
>> bogging down the vectorization.
>
> And my guess is that with enough functions vectorized, the covariance matrix computation could be fully vectorized when written in Stan language so that the expression tree would be smallish and it would be quite fast even without internal C++ implementation of the covariance function...

But the current vectorization of functions doesn't cut
down expression tree size --- it's just a loop on the
inside of the function instead of int he Stan language,
which doesn't matter for efficiency.

The vectorized distributions are another matter --- those
do create just one new node (with an edge to each input --- the
complexity is a multiply-add per edge, and also a virtual function
call for each node).

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] finishing a covariance function implementation (for GPs)
parts:
I think what we really want down the road is
a function that returns the Cholesky decomposition
of the covariance matrix directly, and at that point
we could wrap everything up in a single (matrix-valued)
node on the expression graph, no?

The nice feature of this design is that if we get
structured covariance matrices then we can use
structured solvers behind the scenes (once we have
support for structured solvers, etc…)

>>>
>>> And my guess is that with enough functions vectorized, the covariance matrix computation could be fully vectorized when written in Stan language so that the expression tree would be smallish and it would be quite fast even without internal C++ implementation of the covariance function...
>>
>> But the current vectorization of functions doesn't cut
>> down expression tree size --- it's just a loop on the
>> inside of the function instead of int he Stan language,
>> which doesn't matter for efficiency.
>
> Oh :(
> Thanks for pointing this out.
>
> Aki
>
>>
>> The vectorized distributions are another matter --- those
>> do create just one new node (with an edge to each input --- the
>> complexity is a multiply-add per edge, and also a virtual function
>> call for each node).
>>
>> - Bob

> > > > a function that returns the Cholesky decomposition
> > > > of the covariance matrix directly, and at that point
> > > > we could wrap everything up in a single (matrix-valued)
> > > > node on the expression graph, no?
> > > >
> > > > The nice feature of this design is that if we get
> > > > structured covariance matrices then we can use
> > > > structured solvers behind the scenes (once we have
> > > > support for structured solvers, etc…)
> > > >
> > > >> On May 24, 2016, at 11:21 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
> > > >>
> > > >> On Tuesday, May 24, 2016 at 3:43:20 AM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > >>>> On May 23, 2016, at 4:04 AM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:
> > > >>>>
> > > >>>>> On Monday, May 23, 2016 at 5:13:19 AM UTC+3, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > >>>>> Devin doesn't know C++ yet and this one's hairy or Daniel would be
> > > >>>>> done with already. All these higher-order tests are also what's
> > > >>>>> bogging down the vectorization.
> > > >>>>
> > > >>>> And my guess is that with enough functions vectorized, the covariance matrix computation could be fully vectorized when written in Stan language so that the expression tree would be smallish and it would be quite fast even without internal C++ implementation of the covariance function...
> > > >>>
> > > >>> But the current vectorization of functions doesn't cut
> > > >>> down expression tree size --- it's just a loop on the
> > > >>> inside of the function instead of int he Stan language,
> > > >>> which doesn't matter for efficiency.
> > > >>
> > > >> Oh :(
> > > >> Thanks for pointing this out.
> > > >>
> > > >> Aki
> > > >>
> > > >>>
> > > >>> The vectorized distributions are another matter --- those
> > > >>> do create just one new node (with an edge to each input --- the
> > > >>> complexity is a multiply-add per edge, and also a virtual function
> > > >>> call for each node).
> > > >>>
> > > >>> - Bob
